title: Ivan Kotliarevskyi
summary: Ivan Petrovych Kotliarevsky was a prominent Ukrainian writer, poet, playwright, and social activist, recognized as the pioneer of modern Ukrainian literature. His notable work, the poem Eneida, is a travesty of Virgil's Aeneid and marks a significant milestone in the use of vernacular Ukrainian as a literary language.

sections.heading: Biography
paragraphs: Ivan Petrovych Kotliarevsky was born on 9 September [O.S. 29 August] 1769 in [[poltava|Poltava]], [[ukraine|Ukraine]], to a family of clerk Petro Kotliarevsky. While the Kotliarevskys were part of the [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] nobility, they were not affluent, owning a small estate in Poltava and additional land nearby. He attended the Poltava Theological Seminary from 1780 to 1789 and subsequently worked as a tutor for the gentry, which allowed him to gain insight into Ukrainian folk life and the peasant vernacular.

Kotliarevsky served in the Imperial Russian Army from 1796 to 1808 in the Siversky Karabiner Regiment and participated in the Russo-Turkish War (1806–1812) as a staff-captain, notably during the siege of Izmail. He retired from military service in 1808 and became a trustee of an educational institution for impoverished noble children in 1810. In 1812, amidst the French invasion of Russia, he organized the 5th Ukrainian Cossack Regiment in Horoshyn, Poltava Governorate, with the intention of establishing it as a permanent military unit, earning the rank of major.

Kotliarevsky was involved in theatrical productions at the Poltava governor-general's residence and served as the artistic director of the Poltava Free Theater from 1812 to 1821. He joined the Poltava Freemasonry Lodge Liubov do istyny (Love of truth) in 1818, alongside Vasyl Lukashevych and V. Taranovsky. He played a role in the buyout of actor Mikhail Shchepkin from serfdom. From 1827 to 1835, he directed several philanthropic agencies. Kotliarevsky passed away on 10 November [O.S. 29 October] 1838 and was interred in Poltava after freeing his serfs and distributing his property to relatives and acquaintances.

sections.heading: The First Modern Ukrainian Writer
paragraphs: Kotliarevsky began writing poetry during his time at the Poltava Theological Seminary, with his early works published in the satirical almanac Poltavska mukha (Poltava fly). He initiated his most famous literary piece, the travesty poem Eneida (Ukrainian: Енеїда), in 1794. The initial three parts were published in Saint Petersburg in 1798 without his consent, marking the beginning of modern [[ukrainian-literature|Ukrainian literature]] as it was the first significant use of vernacular Ukrainian as a literary language. The fourth part was released in 1809, and the fifth and sixth parts were completed around 1820, though the first complete edition was published posthumously in 1842.

Eneida draws upon the tradition of travesties of Virgil's Aeneid found in European literature, particularly inspired by Nikolay Osipov's earlier work Aeneid Turned Inside Out. However, Kotliarevsky's rendition uniquely transforms the Trojan heroes into [[zaporozhian-cossacks|Zaporozhian Cossacks]] and depicts the Olympian gods as oppressive landlords, reflecting the historical context of the [[zaporizhian-sich|Zaporozhian Sich]]'s destruction and the prevalence of serfdom in Ukraine. The poem satirizes various social classes and gained immense popularity, influencing numerous imitations. Additionally, Kotliarevsky introduced accentual-syllabic verse into Ukrainian poetry, favoring it over the earlier syllabic form, and utilized iambic tetrameter in structured strophes.
His two plays, Natalka Poltavka (Natalka from Poltava, 1819) and Moskal-Charivnyk (The soldier-sorcerer), significantly contributed to the evolution of Ukrainian national theater.

sections.heading: Views
paragraphs: Pavlo Petrenko notes that Kotliarevsky's worldview was primarily driven by moral considerations rather than sociopolitical factors. His empathy towards the socially and nationally oppressed Ukrainian peasantry was often secondary to his allegiance to the tsarist autocracy.

sections.heading: Legacy
paragraphs: Kotliarevsky's influence is evident in the works of his successors, including Hryhorii Kvitka-Osnovianenko, [[taras-shevchenko|Taras Shevchenko]], and others, as well as in the ethnographic plays of the late 19th century. His impact extended to Russian literature, influencing figures such as [[nikolai-gogol|Nikolai Gogol]] and Vasilii Narezhny, and even Belarusian literature with the anonymous Eneida navyvarat.

His complete works were published in [[kyiv|Kyiv]] between 1952 and 1953 and again in 1969. The Kotliarevsky Museum was established in Poltava in 1952. The [[kharkiv-oblast|Kharkiv]] I. P. Kotlyarevsky National University of Arts is named in his honor. Monuments commemorating Kotliarevsky can be found in Kyiv and Poltava, and numerous streets and boulevards across Ukrainian cities bear his name, with significant ones located in Kyiv, Poltava, and other major cities.

sections.heading: English Translations
paragraphs: The first few stanzas of Kotliarevsky's Eneida were translated into English by Wolodymyr Semenyna and published in the Ukrainian Weekly on 20 October 1933. However, the first complete English translation of the work was not published until 2004 by Ukrainian-Canadian Bohdan Melnyk.
